## Delivery guide

This script accompanies the [RDD deck](rdd.qmd) and its
[RevealJS version](rdd-revealjs.html). Allow 45-60 minutes for the cover and 21
main content slides, with two optional appendix slides and references. Learners
should know basic regression. The three R labs are separate practical sessions.
The [core report](../labs/regression-discontinuity-methods-report.qmd) supplies
the executable calculations and a longer account of assumptions.

## Main sequence

### Cover: Regression Discontinuity

Introduce the question: when can an administrative threshold provide a causal
comparison? Ask learners to keep one eligibility rule in mind throughout.

### 1. The rule creates the comparison

Allow 2 minutes. Elicit an actual rule and identify its score. Explain that RD
starts with institutional knowledge rather than an outcome plot. The end goal is
a local causal claim with a defensible interpretation [@gertler2016ch6rdd].

### 2. Write down the assignment mechanism

Allow 2 minutes. Separate score measurement, eligibility, receipt, and outcome.
Ask whether a revised score could differ from the one used to assign treatment.
Ask what other benefits use the same threshold.

### 3. Sharp and fuzzy designs answer different questions

Allow 2 minutes. A sharp design determines receipt; a fuzzy design changes receipt
probability. The latter requires an IV argument, not just a rescaled sharp label.
Defer the ratio until participants understand the sharp comparison.

### 4. PANES provides a sharp teaching case

Allow 2 minutes. Explain the 1,948-observation outcome sample and the three-valued
support measure. Clarify that this is a programme package and a teaching snapshot,
not an isolated cash-payment effect or a full replication [@manacorda2011transfers].

### 5. Treatment is on the left

Allow 2 minutes. Have learners predict the sign of a right-minus-left coefficient
if treatment raises support. Resolve the sign convention before introducing any
estimated effects. Ask how the interval must transform too.

### 6. Continuity supplies the missing outcome

Allow 3 minutes. Discuss a coincident policy, precise sorting, and outcome selection
as different threats. Continuity permits slopes and levels to vary away from the
cutoff. Neither sample size nor significance proves it [@cunningham2021rdd].

### 7. The effect is local

Allow 2 minutes. Read the two limits, then reverse their order for left-side
treatment. Ask whether an effect near eligibility can represent all programme
participants. Distinguish identification from external validity.

### 8. Plot the score before choosing a model

Allow 2 minutes. Identify bins, the true cutoff, and the shorter fitted window.
Explain why bin width is not regression bandwidth and why bins must not span the
threshold. A high-order curve is not evidence of a better design.

### 9. A local line makes the jump inspectable

Allow 3 minutes. Set score to zero in the formula to recover the intercept jump.
Explain triangular weights and separate slopes. The h=0.01 calculation uses 537
left and 400 right observations and agrees with the foundations lab.

### 10. Bandwidth trades approximation against information

Allow 2 minutes. Ask what is lost by narrowing and widening the window. Automatic
selection optimizes a statistical criterion, not assignment validity. Distinct
nearby scores are important even when the number of people is large.

### 11. Bias-aware inference changes what is reported

Allow 3 minutes. Explain the difference between the +0.0335 conventional estimate
and -0.0416 corrected estimate. The robust interval is for the bias-aware procedure.
Do not choose a sign or report percentage points for the nonbinary support score.

### 12. Sensitivity belongs beside the estimate

Allow 2 minutes. Compare rows as different local approximations, not competing
significance tests. Both h and b change together in this figure. The responsible
conclusion is local and imprecise under these specifications.

### 13. Density evidence needs the right sample

Allow 2 minutes. Explain the separate 52,549-score file and the 20,463 near-cutoff
observations. Ask how outcome-survey selection could distort a density test.
Non-rejection is not proof of no sorting.

### 14. Covariate checks require a timeline

Allow 2 minutes. The timing of Age and Education is not established as pre-treatment.
Education has 51 missing values. Use variable-specific samples and avoid describing
post-treatment or uncertain-timing variables as baseline balance.

### 15. Placebos and donuts test specific concerns

Allow 2 minutes. Give a placebo at 0.01 with h=b=0.004 as a same-regime example.
A donut removes the closest comparisons and increases reliance on extrapolation.
Require a substantive reason for each check rather than a checklist of p-values.

### 16. Fuzzy RD uses two discontinuities

Allow 2 minutes. Introduce the separate veteran-status application and its binary
homeownership outcome. The first stage falls from left to right. Point out the
discrete quarter support in the plot [@fetter2013mortgages].

### 17. The local Wald ratio connects outcome and receipt

Allow 3 minutes. Divide both right-minus-left jumps using identical weights and
samples. The conventional estimate is approximately 18.63 percentage points.
Explain that reversing only one jump gives the wrong sign; ordinary regression
on fitted treatment does not supply valid IV standard errors.

### 18. Fuzzy identification adds assumptions

Allow 3 minutes. Ask for a non-mortgage pathway from veteran status to homeownership
to motivate exclusion. Define local compliers and direction-consistent monotonicity.
The code's minimum first-stage magnitude is a numerical guard, not an inferential
weak-instrument test [@huntingtonklein2025rdd].

### 19. Many people do not create continuous support

Allow 2 minutes. Contrast 56,901 records with only 12 distinct quarters on each
side. More records at a score do not create values nearer zero. Do not apply a
continuous density test or assume quarter clustering repairs extrapolation bias.

### 20. Report the design and its limits

Allow 2 minutes. Ask learners for a short conclusion that states the local
population, effect and uncertainty, and one unresolved threat. A bounded claim
is more informative than a programme-wide interpretation the data cannot support.

### 21. Three R labs continue the sequence

Allow 1 minute. Direct learners to sharp foundations first, diagnostics second,
and fuzzy RD last. Each has Quarto, an R Jupyter notebook, local data, and a ZIP.
Ask for a written design assessment before interpreting the regression output.

## Optional appendix

The first appendix distinguishes estimation and bias bandwidths and explains why
both appear in the report. The second distinguishes the conventional fuzzy ratio
from the corrected effect and robust interval. Keep the coarse-support limitation
visible even when the interval excludes zero.

## Discussion answers

- A threshold can identify the effect of a package when several services change together; it cannot isolate each component without more information.
- An insignificant density or covariate test is compatible with limited power and does not establish continuity.
- A donut can address a specific data concern but changes the information used to extrapolate to the cutoff.
- A fuzzy estimate concerns local compliers under additional IV assumptions, not every participant.
- An apparently precise result can still have an implausible assignment argument or insufficiently dense score support.
